project_type: Authenticated web SaaS — document processing / PDF-to-Q&A extraction with human-in-the-loop review
project_description: Users authenticate via Auth0, upload a PDF and declare its copyright status. An upstream pipeline extracts question-and-answer pairs from the document's paragraph structure. Users review and edit the pairs in-browser, mark editing complete, and download the finished set as a Word document. Subscriptions run through Stripe.

verified_claims.claim: Rebuilt a Lambda-hosted API layer: removed an ORM and a per-cold-start schema sync from the cold path, eliminated a connection-pool leak that could stall requests for up to 30 seconds, externalised hardcoded production credentials, and standardised on parameterised SQL in a layered service.
verified_claims.evidence: Archived src/app.ts and src/db.ts: un-awaited and never-released app.pg.connect() in the /alldocuments handler; sequelize.sync() in a floating Promise at module load; pool acquire timeout 30000ms with max 10; connection string hardcoded. Versus 2024-backend-pdf2qa: 32 pool-managed app.pg.query() call sites, zero pg.connect() calls, connection string in POSTGRES_CONNECTION_STRING.
verified_claims.qualification: The mechanisms are verified from the code and can be claimed without reservation. Authorship of the prior version is not established. The latency figure is a separate claim — see C3a.

verified_claims.claim: The rebuild reduced API response time from seconds to milliseconds.
verified_claims.evidence: Six independently verifiable defects in the archived pre-rewrite implementation, each plausibly costing hundreds of milliseconds to seconds under the testing method used; all six removed by the rewrite.
defects_found: Two separate connection pools to the same RDS instance (a Sequelize pool and a registered @fastify/postgres pool)
Sequelize pool configured min: 0 with idle: 10000 — no warm connections held, idle connections evicted after ten seconds
acquire: 30000 — pool contention surfaces as a 30-second stall rather than a fast failure
The /alldocuments handler called app.pg.connect() without await and never released the client — simultaneously broken and leaking a pool slot per call
Five handlers call client.release() twice on the same client; releasing an already-released pg client throws
sequelize.sync() invoked in a floating, unawaited Promise at module load, issuing DDL round trips per registered model
verified_claims.qualification: Direction and order of magnitude follow from the code itself, independent of anyone's memory. The precise figures are a separate claim — see C3b.

verified_claims.claim: Specifically, average response time fell from approximately 11 seconds to approximately 110 milliseconds.

verified_claims.remaining_limitation: No record of the measurement was kept. The claim rests on recollection of a consistent comparison, not on a preserved benchmark.

engineering_challenges.challenge: Communicating asynchronous pipeline state to a synchronous UI with no event feed
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Each solution trades differently: load-time fetch is free but stale within seconds; per-document 30s polling is correct but scales as documents x users against a per-invocation-billed Lambda; a WebSocket delta service centralises the poll but introduces a stateful long-lived process that does not fit the Lambda model.

engineering_challenges.challenge: Deleting a user across three systems with no distributed transaction
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Auth0, PostgreSQL and S3 cannot participate in one transaction. The chosen ordering fails safe on Auth0 rejection but still orphans local rows if the process crashes mid-cascade.

engineering_challenges.challenge: Fastify's single-lifecycle model versus Lambda's container reuse
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Duplicate route registration only fails on warm starts, so it passes local testing and first deploy.

engineering_challenges.challenge: Lambda package size with Fastify + aws-sdk + pg + auth0
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Bundling dependencies with function code makes every deploy slow and risks the unzipped size limit; splitting required five coordinated npm scripts and hand-written SDK deployment code.

engineering_challenges.challenge: Leaf-first ordered deletion across a four-level foreign-key hierarchy
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Each level is reachable only through correlated subqueries from a single documentId; wrong order gives FK violations, wrong transaction boundary leaves orphans.

engineering_challenges.challenge: Inheriting and consolidating a multi-author codebase
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Three overlapping UI libraries (MUI 5, Material-UI 4, Reactstrap) and a duplicated component file left by a rotating team of 19.

decisions.problem: Low, bursty API traffic alongside an existing serverless pipeline
decisions.decision: Run the HTTP API as Fastify on AWS Lambda rather than a container
decisions.reasoning: Pay-per-invocation economics; the team already ran ECS for the frontend and chose per workload
decisions.tradeoffs: Cold starts on an RDS-backed API; no cross-invocation connection pooling (many containers can exhaust RDS connections); Fastify lifecycle needed an initialisation guard
decisions.result: Worked, with complexity pushed into the deployment pipeline

decisions.problem: Account deletion needs outbound internet to Auth0; the main API needs VPC access to RDS
decisions.decision: Separate the deletion endpoint into its own Lambda and API Gateway
decisions.reasoning: Avoid provisioning a NAT gateway for the whole API
decisions.tradeoffs: A second deployable, gateway and frontend base URL; the deletion route still queries RDS

decisions.problem: File bytes through a Lambda API cost money and hit payload limits
decisions.decision: Presigned S3 URLs for all transfer in both directions
decisions.reasoning: Keeps the API stateless and small
decisions.tradeoffs: The API never validates file contents; a presigned PUT is a trusted write; the upload presign has no explicit expiry (download has 30s)

decisions.problem: Every browser polling independently is wasteful
decisions.decision: A standalone WebSocket service that polls the REST API once and pushes deltas
decisions.reasoning: No event bus exists to subscribe to, so something must poll; centralise it
decisions.tradeoffs: Single point of failure; process-local status map prevents horizontal scaling; still 5s latency and constant upstream load with no changes; pipeline-published events would remove polling entirely
decisions.result: Built on a branch; no evidence of production deployment

decisions.problem: Routine Lambda deploys shipped tens of megabytes
decisions.reasoning: Keep function-code deploys small and version dependencies independently
decisions.tradeoffs: Layer and code can drift if package.json changes without a layer rebuild
decisions.result: Deploys reduced to kilobytes of function code

decisions.problem: Where to host the Next.js app
decisions.decision: Container to ECR/ECS rather than Vercel or Amplify
decisions.reasoning: Keeps the whole product in one AWS account under one IAM model
decisions.tradeoffs: A container build and an always-on service for an app that could have run serverless
decisions.result: GitHub Actions pipeline on push to dev

problems_solved.solution: Interval polling scoped to non-terminal documents only, then a WebSocket delta-push service

security_findings.publication_guidance: Discuss these as your own retrospective in interviews. Never publish them tied to an identifiable system, even a decommissioned one.

lessons: Polling is a legitimate first answer and a bad last one — the step not taken (pipeline-published events) would have removed polling entirely
Commenting out an authorisation check is how security holes ship; a comment is not a TODO and will not come back
A CI pipeline that cannot fail is worse than none, because it looks like a safety net
Serverless pushes complexity into deployment; the cost is invisible at architecture time and very visible six weeks later
Inherited frontends accumulate UI libraries; three coexisted here and consolidation never beat features
Build dashboards against the real API from day one — this one looks finished and shows fabricated numbers
A decommissioned product erases your evidence; capture a production metrics snapshot while the system is alive

interview_stories.title: Volunteering for the problem nobody else could take
interview_stories.situation: The API was slow and it was a recurring topic in team discussions. The cloud architect on the project was an AWS solutions specialist rather than a hands-on Node developer, so the problem sat unowned between disciplines.
interview_stories.task: Nobody had picked it up; the subject volunteered because Node.js was his area.
interview_stories.action: Read the existing implementation, found six distinct defects, and rebuilt the service rather than patching around them.
interview_stories.result: Response times went from seconds to milliseconds when tested the same way before and after.
interview_stories.evidence: The archived pre-rewrite code and the repository created three days later. The organisational context is the SUBJECT'S ACCOUNT — the Microsoft Teams history is no longer accessible to him.
interview_stories.why_it_is_strong: Not 'I was assigned a performance ticket' but 'a problem sat unowned between disciplines, I recognised it was in my area, and I took it.' Deliver the organisational context as narrative and the six defects as specifics; the specifics make it credible.

interview_stories.title: The same problem, solved three times
interview_stories.situation: Documents processed asynchronously; the UI showed stale status
interview_stories.task: Keep users informed with no event feed from the pipeline
interview_stories.action: Load-time fetch, then per-document 30s polling excluding terminal states, then a WebSocket service holding a server-side status map polling upstream once every 5s and pushing only diffs
interview_stories.result: Live status with one upstream poll per connection instead of one per document per client
interview_stories.follow_up: What now? Publish events from the pipeline and drop polling; move the status map out of process memory

portfolio_material.overview: Qutii turned PDF documents into reviewable, editable question-and-answer sets, with a human-in-the-loop review step between automated extraction and a .docx download.
portfolio_material.challenge: The product sat on top of an asynchronous pipeline the web tier had no visibility into and no event feed from. Everything hard followed from that: communicating state, preventing action on in-flight documents, and cleaning up across a relational database, object storage and a third-party identity provider.
portfolio_material.role: Frontend began May 2023 with up to 19 contributors. From April 2024 the subject was the only person committing to it, and in May 2024 created the backend API repository from scratch and remained its principal author.
portfolio_material.solution: Fastify API in TypeScript on AWS Lambda behind API Gateway, PostgreSQL on RDS, presigned S3 transfer, Auth0 identity with JWT-scoped queries, a separate Lambda for account deletion needing outbound internet access, a standalone WebSocket status service, and a hand-built deployment pipeline.
portfolio_material.results: The full lifecycle shipped and ran in production. No production metrics survive; the environment was decommissioned before this audit.
what_id_improve: Have the pipeline publish status events to SNS/EventBridge instead of polling anything

ai_positioning.weak_avoid: 'Worked on an AI product' — true but claims nothing and invites the question you do not want to answer vaguely.
ai_positioning.interview_script: The extraction model itself was owned by another part of the team — I didn't build or call it. What I owned was everything around it: getting documents in, orchestrating jobs that took minutes rather than milliseconds, surfacing failure states, and building the review workflow, because the generated pairs needed human correction before anyone would trust them. A few hundred pairs per document, all editable, with the approval gate before release.
ai_positioning.where_the_integration_claim_belongs: A separate freelance engagement in which the subject states he genuinely integrated AI into a client's system. Keeping the two distinct is what makes both credible: this project supplies AI PLATFORM experience with nine months of verifiable ownership; that project should supply AI INTEGRATION experience with model names and integration patterns.
ai_positioning.recommended_next_step: Run this same evidence audit against that freelance project to produce evidenced AI-integration claims.
